paper_title: Minimizing Tardy Processing Time on a Single Machine in Near-Linear Time
statement: It remains an interesting open question whether our O(P e )-time algorithm can be further improved with respect to the parameters dmax and pmax . In principle it seems reasonable that time O(n+d e max ) can be achieved, as the analogous question for Subset Sum is resolved [8, 26]. We leave this as an open question. An even more exciting question is whether we could possibly achieve time O(ne + pmax ). However, such an algorithm would entail a break-through for Subset Sum with small items, which currently seems out of reach.
context: There has been research on developing nontrivial 1|| pj Uj algorithms (for a single machine) with respect to these parameters, such as an O(min{P e ·D# , P +D})-time algorithm 3 due to [12], and an O(n + pmax )-time algorithm due to [28]. We remark that the former is e subsumed by our new results. The latter algorithm is incomparable to our result (specifically, 1/2 our algorithm in time O(P max ) performs better if and only if pmax ≫ n e ) = O(np e ). Both of these results [12, 28] generalize to m machines as well, leading to similar comparisons with our work. It remains an interesting open question whether our O(P e )-time algorithm can be further improved with respect to the parameters dmax and pmax . In principle it seems reasonable that time O(n+d e max ) can be achieved, as the analogous question for Subset Sum is resolved [8, 26]. We leave this as an open question. An even more exciting question is whether we could possibly achieve time O(ne + pmax ). However, such an algorithm would entail a break-through for Subset Sum with small items, which currently seems out of reach. Further Related Work. This work is part of a bigger effort of the fine-grained complexity community to design best-possible pseudo-polynomial time algorithms for a host of optimization problems. This line of research encompasses, besides the aforementioned scheduling problems [12, 23, 28, 36], various variants of Subset Sum [29, 8, 1, 5, 6, 13, 33, 4, 14, 34, 19], Knapsack [38, 18, 30, 7, 20, 33, 11, 16, 10, 9, 25], Integer Programming [20, 24] and many others [15, 19]. 2 Preliminaries Throughout, we write [n] = {0, . . . , n − 1} and use the interval notation [i . . j] = {i, . . . , j}, and similarly [i . . j), (i . . j], (i . . j). For two sets of integers S, T and an integer t we employ the sumset notation S + t = {s + t : s ∈ S} and S + T = {s + t : s ∈ S, t ∈ T }.
